items.followUp: State two differences between Rutherford’s model and Bohr’s model of the atom.

rubric.why: The models differ in the paths and energy levels allowed for electrons.
rubric.description: Contrasts Rutherford’s electrons revolving at any distance with Bohr’s electrons occupying fixed orbits or definite energy levels.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly contrasting the electron orbits or energy levels in the two models.

rubric.why: Bohr’s stationary orbits explain atomic stability, which Rutherford’s model could not explain.
rubric.description: Contrasts Rutherford’s inability to explain atomic stability with Bohr’s stationary orbits, in which electrons do not radiate energy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct contrast about stability or energy radiation in the two models.

modelAnswer: In Rutherford’s model, electrons can revolve around the nucleus at any distance; in Bohr’s model, electrons revolve in fixed orbits with definite energy levels.
Rutherford’s model could not explain the stability of the atom; Bohr proposed that electrons in stationary orbits do not radiate energy.

items.followUp: Why are the elements of the f-block shown in two rows below the main body of the periodic table?

rubric.why: Separating the series prevents the periodic table from becoming too wide.
rubric.description: Explains that the separate placement saves space or keeps the table compact and manageable in width.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a valid explanation based on the table’s size or layout.

rubric.why: The two series belong to the sixth and seventh periods, respectively.
rubric.description: Identifies the lanthanides as belonging to period 6 and the actinides as belonging to period 7.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly connecting both series to their respective periods.

modelAnswer: Lanthanides and actinides are placed separately below the periodic table to save space and keep the table compact.
The lanthanides belong to the sixth period and the actinides to the seventh period.

items.followUp: Define a suspension and give one example.

accept: homogeneous mixture of solute and solvent
rubric.why: A solution is a homogeneous mixture of its components.
rubric.description: Defines a solution as a homogeneous mixture of a solute and a solvent.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct definition.

rubric.why: A suitable example demonstrates the meaning of a solution.
rubric.description: Gives a valid example of a solution, such as salt or sugar dissolved in water.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct example.

modelAnswer: A solution is a homogeneous mixture of a solute and a solvent.
Salt dissolved in water is an example of a solution.
